messages.subject: A newbie's experience using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
I just sent off a report that consistent of 15 charts created with
ggplot2.  ggplot2 was a very valuable tool. The first time I used it
was 2 weeks ago, so I wanted to report on my experience, Hadley,
because it might be useful as you revise the book.  I probably have
read the book four times during the last two weeks.  Perhaps this
account also might be helpful to someone else who is just starting
with ggplot2.

The plots I did were quite basic in terms of sstatistics: simple time
series lines with no statistic more complicated than just a sum
counting numbers of people, broken down into various subgroups.  I
used ggplot2 because I wanted nice looking charts and because I was
looking for a practical way to follow-up on what I learned taking
Tufte’s course this fall.  In particular, I wanted to produce small
multiples.  I made extensive use of facet_wrap and it worked well for
me. I ended up with something that I think looked more classy than
what I would have gotten using lattice.

What are the things I had the most trouble with?  Section 4.5.2 was
crucial and it took me a while before I realized I had to zero in on
those pages and really understand what was going on.  When using
geom_point, geom_text, and so on I struggled a bit to understand what
needed to be in the aes function. The fact that aes gets referred to
functionally as mapping probably slowed me down a tad. I actually
ended up doing a bit of trial and error.  For example, I haven’t been
consistent about using I(“colour”) inside aes versus just setting
colour in the call outside of aes. See the comment in the code at the
end of the message for one geom_text where I inquire about why colour
needs I() but size did not.

The “Build a plot layer by layer” chapter was crucial for me, but I
needed to know a certain amount before I could digest the significance
of what I was being told. I needed an advanced recap of “build a plot
layer by layer” at the end of the book, although going back and re-
reading things a couple of times accomplished the same thing.  Also
after I got going I started using the summary function more and
relating that to what I was reading in the “build a plot” chapter and
things started to make more sense.

One thing I would have liked would have been a real help file for layer
() and ggplot() and for aes(). Going down to that level helped with my
attempts to understand how things related.  The web reference manual
was invaluable and I would have been lost without it.  I also needed
to use the R code for the figures in the book that was provided as
separate files.

Because I wanted to make fairly heavy use of annotations (inspired in
part by Tufte), section 5.9 turned out to be crucial.  I had to go
over that several times before I was relatively clear about what I
needed to do for annotations. It’s an effective an example which
covers a variety of annotations.

I think I’m still a bit unclear about the relationship between
geom_xxx and stat_yyy.  I used cast() to sum up the counts for my
plots.  I think I  might have been able to do the same using sum with
a stat function, but my one feeble attempt at that didn’t work and cast
() was getting the job done for me so I didn’t pursue it.

What would my ggplot2 future version wish list be after my
experience?

With facet_wrap, it would be nice to have a wee bit more control over
how facets appear.  Right now the choice is to have a fully crossed
layout or to have a filled wrap.  But in my case it would have been
useful to be able to have facet_wrap skip some cases and go to the
next row. In that way I could have kept some related charts together
on the same row in a way not captured by a fully crossed layout. I
think lattice can do something like that.

I would like to have used expand= so that I made room only at the
right side of the chart rather than symmetrically. In a couple of
places I put annotations at the end of a trend line and I wanted to
make room for them via expand.

In a number of cases with my annotations overplotting of the text was
an issue. In some cases I handled that by manually adjusting the x and
y position. I was thinking about what I would need to do to write a
function that would accomplish a bit of that automatically. (I’ve done
that in Java with another set of plots that I do where I make
extensive use of labeled points.) The trick here is that I don’t know
the size of the text in the label so I don’t know how much of an
adjustment I have to make in the x and y coordinates. I’ll think about
this one some more.  Presumably I might be able to do something with
grid, but I want to avoid going there if at all possible. My ideal
would be a geom_text_point that would add text labels to points and
would do something jitter-like to attempt to minimize over-writing of
text. Maybe I'll take a stab at that some day.

What else did I learn?  Daniel Webster and others did us Yankees a
favor by simplifying spelling. But I have to admit that the British
Commonwealth has a point in sticking with "colour."  The two o's
aren't pronounced the same way. Working with ggplot2 forced me to
think about that. A lot.

All in all, I had a very rewarding experience with ggplot2.  It's a
great piece of work and I look forward to making even more use of it.
You've also done a very good job with the book.

Below is the code I used to produce one of the 15 figures.  I’m
including the code not because I think it’s a model, but because I
thought you might be interested to see the weirdness someone might
come up with after diving into the book for two weeks and having only
a partial idea of how things work with ggplot2 (and R as well).

-- John Goldin

# because I was creating multiple figures, I used variables as
# I set various things so as to be consistent across figures.
label.size<-2.5
label.size.large <- 3
small.point=1.25
# setup color scale by modifying a brewed scale
require(RColorBrewer)
cset<-brewer.pal(11,"RdBu")
# I used this color.choice list to get consistent colors across
figures that
# included various subgroups.
color.choice <- c("M&P" = cset[1],"C&T" = cset[2], "S&M"=cset[4],
"Staff"=cset[2],
	"Tenured"=cset[11], "Term"=cset[9], "Ladder" =cset[10], "Non-
Ladder"="darkorange",
	"Research"="darkgoldenrod", "Faculty"=cset[10], "Trainee"="green")
choose.level1 = "Prof Schls"
# make_relative is a function I wrote that adds some labels and some
other
# calculations to the cast
ds <- make_relative(cast(subset(srt.melt2,level1==choose.level1),
	simple + year + unit ~ variable, sum),
	limit.revised=rev.limit, min.size=cell.floor,sep.source=F)
# calculate staff to faculty ratio based on ds for total chart
ds$staff.faculty.ratio<-NA
ds$staff.faculty.ratio[ds$simple=="Faculty"] <- mapply(function(a,b){
	if(b>0){return(a/b)}else{return(NA)}},
	ds$fte[ds$simple=="Staff"], ds$fte[ds$simple=="Faculty"])
p <- qplot(year, fte, data=ds, geom=c("line"),
	colour=simple,main="FTE's by School",
	xlab=set.xlab, ylab = "FTE's", ymin=0)+scale_colour_hue("Type")
# I put geom_point separate from geom in qplot because I wanted to
specificy a size
p<-p+geom_point(data=ds,size=small.point,aes(x=year,
y=fte,colour=simple, shape=simple))
p<-p+scale_shape("Type")
p<- p+scale_colour_manual(values=color.choice[levels(factor(ds
$simple))])
# note expand to make room for annotations at the end of the trend
line
p <- p + scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(2000,last.year,by=4),expand=c
(0,exp.size))+
	scale_y_continuous(formatter=comma)
# turning off the legend turned out to be crucial
p<-p+geom_text(legend=F,data=ds[(ds$year==2008),],aes(
	x=year+0.1, y=fte, colour=simple, hjust=0, vjust=0,
label=fte.label),size=label.size)
# print the number 5 years ago
p<-p+geom_text(legend=F,data=ds[(ds$year==(2008-5)),],aes(
	x=year+0.1, y=fte+3, colour=simple, hjust=.5, vjust=0,
label=fte.label),size=label.size)
# add a 5 year percentage increase to the last number
p<-p+geom_text(legend=F,data=ds[(ds$year==2008) ,],aes(
	x=year+0.1, y=fte-2, colour=simple, hjust=0, vjust=1,
label=pct.increase),size=label.size)
p<-p+facet_wrap( ~ unit)+opts(axis.text.x=theme_text
(colour="darkgrey",size=8,vjust=1))
# add line for Law Lib to the Law School panel
detail<-make_relative(cast(subset(srt.melt2,(level1==choose.level1) &
	(orgname == "Law Sch Library") & (simple=="Staff")),
	simple + year + unit ~ variable, sum),
	limit.revised=rev.limit, min.size=cell.floor, sep.source=F)
detail$label <- ""
detail$label[detail$year==2002]<-"Law Library"
p<-p + geom_line(data=detail, aes(x=year, y=fte),colour=I
("lightgreen"))
# in the next geom_text, why does colour have to I() but size does
not?
p<-p +geom_text(data=detail, aes(label=label, vjust=0),colour=I
("lightgreen"),size=3)
p<-p + geom_point(data=detail, aes(x=year, y=fte, shape=simple),
colour=I("lightgreen"),
	size=small.point, legend=F))
# I found .eps worked best for inserting into Microsoft Word on
Windows
# Using gsave turned out to be my best bet for getting constant sizes
for my
# various figures.
ggsave(p, paste(this.dir,file.level1,".eps",sep=""),width=pic_wid,
height=pic_ht)

messages.subject: Re: A newbie's experience using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
I agree on many of John's points.  ggplot2 produces awesome figures
and has immense possibilities.  But from a user perspective, there is
something inherently unintuitive about the instructions for ggplot2
right now (book + website).    On Hadley's website there are lots of
examples, but the code is not throughly explained.  I find working
from examples very useful, only when the code in the example well
explained, otherwise I am just copying without gaining a complete
understanding of it.  With ggplot2 I end up experimenting by modifying
the examples in the book and website...leading to lots of frustration.

The book that I think is really well written for users is 'R Graphics'
by Paul Murrell.  I found his introductory description and explanation
of Lattice more understandable than the Lattice book by Deepayan
Sarkar.  It has few examples, but each example is explained in great
detail.  Buy this I mean, Murrell explains every command in the code
and what it does.

Regards,
Vivek

messages.subject: Re: A newbie's experience using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
As another newbie anxious to master ggplot, I share some of John's
delight and frustrations.  However, I would underscore that the beauty
of Hadley's work is that is sits firmly within a terse and comprehensive
conceptual framework.  Thus, I suspect that the challenges are largely
about navigation and syntax, not conceptual clarity or gaps in the model.

On the issue of navigation, might I suggest a  web-page consisting of
small multiples? Each frame would be one of the graphs (no matter how
trivially different from another) in the book, and each graph would
click to a hypertext link to the associated code. What I am proposing is
like the R-Gallery, but where the search would be primarily/exclusively
visual.  Some ability to add new graphs generated under ggplot, and to
annotate and comment on the code would create an immense resource when
one is struggling to find a comparable example and would allow one to
start to tinker with working code.  Perhaps an adaptation of the
R-Gallery is all that is needed - so that one can focus exclusively on
ggplot graphs.

In my view, the book works very hard to both ease the reader into the
model, the translation of the model into a software design, and finally
the syntax,  but its admirable comprehensiveness makes navigation hard.
(For example, searching to find how to draw boxplots with proportions
took an inordinate amount of time) I  think that rather than a re-write,
some supplemental navigational aids - with code examples, preferably
annotated - would be a great help.

As for syntax, I think that there are some odd bits, notably the (~ .)
syntax in facetting, where the meaning in quite opaque. While I am not
suggesting abandoning that particular syntax, perhaps having another
pathway to achieve the same effect that is less opaque would be helpful.

Rob

messages.subject: opts(aspect.ratio) is incorrect
messages.body_plain:
Hello Hadley,

I'm trying to match my R plots to external data, but this is proving
difficult as the aspect ratio options seems to be based on the frame of
the plot and not the coordinate system.

Take this example:

qplot(x=0,y=0,size=10,xlim=c(-5,5),ylim(-5,5),geom="point") +
opts(aspect.ratio=1) + geom_vline(x=c(-4,4),colour="green",size=1) +
geom_hline(y=c(-4,4),colour="green",size=1)

The grey frame is properly square, but the green lines prove that the
coordinate space is not square at all.

Is there a workaround?

I think it would be best if the padding added to the left and right
edges matched that of the top and bottom edges so that the aspect ratio
of the frame would always match the aspect ratio of the data it contains.

This is in ggplot2 0.8.1

Thanks,
B. Bogart

messages.subject: Re: [R] Time series plots with ggplot
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Feb 3, 2009 at 12:58 PM, Harsh <singh...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
> I am newbie user of ggplot and would like some assistance in
> implementing time series plots.
>
> I'd like to know how the tsdiag plot can be made in ggplot?

It's not particularly easy because the code for tsdiag interweaves
computing statistics and then plotting them.  However, with a bit of
effort you can disentangle them and create the equivalent plots with
ggplot2.

# What does tsdiag look like?
fit <- arima(lh, c(1,0,0))
tsdiag(fit)

# Need to extract the calculations from the existing
# plotting code.  I started by looking at the contents of
# stats:::tsdiag.Arima

# Standardised residuals

stdres <- as.numeric(resid(fit) / sqrt(fit$sigma2))
qplot(seq_along(stdres), stdres, yend = 0, xend = seq_along(stdres),
geom="segment") +
  geom_hline(colour = "grey50")

# ACF

acf <- acf(resid(fit), plot = F)
acf_df <- data.frame(
  acf = acf$acf,
  lag = acf$lag
)
qplot(lag, acf, data = acf_df, yend = 0, xend = lag, geom="segment") +
  geom_hline() + geom_point()

# To figure out the confidence bands, we need to dig into the code
# for stats:::plot.acf.  Unfortunately this isn't available in its own
# method, so I'm not entirely sure I've extracted it correctly
ci <- 0.95
clim <- qnorm((1 + ci)/2) / sqrt(acf$n.used)

qplot(lag, acf, data = acf_df, yend = 0, xend = lag, geom="segment") +
  geom_hline(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-clim, clim), colour = "darkblue")

# Finally the code for the Ljung-Box statistic
ljungbox <- function(i, rs) {
  Box.test(rs, i, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
}
acf_df$pvalue <- sapply(acf_df$lag, ljungbox, series = resid(fit))

qplot(lag, pvalue, data = acf_df) +
  geom_hline(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = "darkblue")

Regards,

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: A newbie's experience using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
> I just sent off a report that consistent of 15 charts created with
> ggplot2.  ggplot2 was a very valuable tool. The first time I used it
> was 2 weeks ago, so I wanted to report on my experience, Hadley,
> because it might be useful as you revise the book.  I probably have
> read the book four times during the last two weeks.  Perhaps this
> account also might be helpful to someone else who is just starting
> with ggplot2.

Great, thanks for your feedback :)

> The plots I did were quite basic in terms of sstatistics: simple time
> series lines with no statistic more complicated than just a sum
> counting numbers of people, broken down into various subgroups.  I
> used ggplot2 because I wanted nice looking charts and because I was
> looking for a practical way to follow-up on what I learned taking
> Tufte's course this fall.  In particular, I wanted to produce small
> multiples.  I made extensive use of facet_wrap and it worked well for
> me. I ended up with something that I think looked more classy than
> what I would have gotten using lattice.
>
> What are the things I had the most trouble with?  Section 4.5.2 was
> crucial and it took me a while before I realized I had to zero in on
> those pages and really understand what was going on.  When using
> geom_point, geom_text, and so on I struggled a bit to understand what
> needed to be in the aes function. The fact that aes gets referred to
> functionally as mapping probably slowed me down a tad. I actually
> ended up doing a bit of trial and error.  For example, I haven't been
> consistent about using I("colour") inside aes versus just setting
> colour in the call outside of aes. See the comment in the code at the
> end of the message for one geom_text where I inquire about why colour
> needs I() but size did not.

You should never use I() in aes - it's only for when you're using qplot.  ie.

qplot(..., colour = I("red"), geom = "point")
is equivalent to
ggplot(...) + geom_point(colour = red))

I know this is confusing and I keep trying to rewrite that section to
make it easier to understand.  I'm still not there yet.

> The "Build a plot layer by layer" chapter was crucial for me, but I
> needed to know a certain amount before I could digest the significance
> of what I was being told. I needed an advanced recap of "build a plot
> layer by layer" at the end of the book, although going back and re-
> reading things a couple of times accomplished the same thing.  Also
> after I got going I started using the summary function more and
> relating that to what I was reading in the "build a plot" chapter and
> things started to make more sense.

Great, I'm glad that function is useful.

> One thing I would have liked would have been a real help file for layer
> () and ggplot() and for aes(). Going down to that level helped with my

Working on the documentation is on my to do list once I have the book
finished.  I agree that good documentation for these key functions
would be very helpful.

> attempts to understand how things related.  The web reference manual
> was invaluable and I would have been lost without it.  I also needed
> to use the R code for the figures in the book that was provided as
> separate files.

The next version of the book will contain substantially more code.  In
the source version of the book all the code to produce the graphics is
interwoven with the text, so I keep forgetting that you don't see the
code when you're reading the book.  I've reread through a printed
version, and I think I've identified most of the places where I need
to insert the code to produce the figures.

> Because I wanted to make fairly heavy use of annotations (inspired in
> part by Tufte), section 5.9 turned out to be crucial.  I had to go
> over that several times before I was relatively clear about what I
> needed to do for annotations. It's an effective an example which
> covers a variety of annotations.

Great.  I have some plans to make annotations even easier to add, but
I don't think they're going to make it before the book deadline.

> I think I'm still a bit unclear about the relationship between
> geom_xxx and stat_yyy.  I used cast() to sum up the counts for my
> plots.  I think I  might have been able to do the same using sum with
> a stat function, but my one feeble attempt at that didn't work and cast
> () was getting the job done for me so I didn't pursue it.

The stats only provide a limited set of statistical transformations,
so if you're happy using reshape, then there's probably no point
changing.

> What would my ggplot2 future version wish list be after my
> experience?
>
> With facet_wrap, it would be nice to have a wee bit more control over
> how facets appear.  Right now the choice is to have a fully crossed
> layout or to have a filled wrap.  But in my case it would have been
> useful to be able to have facet_wrap skip some cases and go to the
> next row. In that way I could have kept some related charts together
> on the same row in a way not captured by a fully crossed layout. I
> think lattice can do something like that.

Maybe I could write a facet_nested which would be a compromise between
the two - it would split into rows based on the first variable and
then in columns by the second, but the columns wouldn't need to be the
same in each row (if that makes any sense!)

> I would like to have used expand= so that I made room only at the
> right side of the chart rather than symmetrically. In a couple of
> places I put annotations at the end of a trend line and I wanted to
> make room for them via expand.

The perfect solution for this would be for geom_text to expand the
axis range based on the position of the text, but unfortunately this
isn't possible in the current ggplot2 scaling pipeline.  As an
alternative to using expand, you can always add invisible points (e.g.
geom_point(colour =NA)) to force the scales out.

> In a number of cases with my annotations overplotting of the text was
> an issue. In some cases I handled that by manually adjusting the x and
> y position. I was thinking about what I would need to do to write a
> function that would accomplish a bit of that automatically. (I've done
> that in Java with another set of plots that I do where I make
> extensive use of labeled points.) The trick here is that I don't know
> the size of the text in the label so I don't know how much of an
> adjustment I have to make in the x and y coordinates. I'll think about
> this one some more.  Presumably I might be able to do something with
> grid, but I want to avoid going there if at all possible. My ideal
> would be a geom_text_point that would add text labels to points and
> would do something jitter-like to attempt to minimize over-writing of
> text. Maybe I'll take a stab at that some day.

I do have some ideas for this on my to do list, but it requires some
fairly deep knowledge of grid and I haven't had a chance to look into
it yet.

> What else did I learn?  Daniel Webster and others did us Yankees a
> favor by simplifying spelling. But I have to admit that the British
> Commonwealth has a point in sticking with "colour."  The two o's
> aren't pronounced the same way. Working with ggplot2 forced me to
> think about that. A lot.
>
> All in all, I had a very rewarding experience with ggplot2.  It's a
> great piece of work and I look forward to making even more use of it.
> You've also done a very good job with the book.

Thanks :)

messages.subject: width, height of a device
messages.body_plain:
This email is both asking for a bit of help and also acting as a
wishlist for a function.

So far I have only used ggplot2 for producing facetted plots. I am
plotting various collections of datasets in various plots. This means
that my plots sometimes have (say) 2x3 facets, sometimes 4x3 and so.
In my case, the content of each facet is the same, so I have identical
x- and y-axis. But since ggplot2 does the standard R thing of
expanding to fill the device, the aspect ratio of the facets on
different plots are different, something that works havoc on any plot-
to-plot comparison.

In standard R I would usually fix this by changing the device size, say
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
quartz(width = 7, height = 7)
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
quartz(width = 14, height = 7)

But in ggplot2 I have two areas, essentially the legend area and also
the axis area to the left side of the plot. This means that if I have
2 columns of facets, I cannot just do facet_width =  device_width / 2

What I would really like is - for a given plot - to tell me how big a
single facet is in width and height in % of the device area. This
should be possible based on my knowledge of grid. At least in the
little grid plotting I have done, I have usually specified sizes in %
of device area, so I am just asking for the right way to interrogate
the ggplot2 structure to get the settings of the facet.

The wishlist function is a function that given a height and a width of
a facet, computes how big the device needs to be in order to get the
given facet height, width. That seems to be very useful for facetted
plotting.

Thanks
Kasper

I get that grobWidth(panel) is equal to 1grobwidth.

My guess is that at this point, the width refers to "the entire grob",

But my grid is a bit rusty, so I am probably wrong.

Kasper

> But unfortunately it gives a width of 0 cm.  I don't understand why,
> so I'll talk to Paul Murrell about it.
>
> What I'm planning for a future release is the complement of your wish
> - the ability to set the width of individual components (e.g. panels
> or legends).  That should make it easier to align multiple plots with
> varying numbers of panels and legends.  It's not currently possible
> because of the way that the viewports are constructed - I first make a
> viewport layout for the panels & axes, and then embed that in another
> viewport for the title, legend and axis labels.
>
> Hadley

>>
>> This email is both asking for a bit of help and also acting as a
>> wishlist for a function.
>>
>> So far I have only used ggplot2 for producing facetted plots. I am
>> plotting various collections of datasets in various plots. This means
>> that my plots sometimes have (say) 2x3 facets, sometimes 4x3 and so.
>> In my case, the content of each facet is the same, so I have

>> expanding to fill the device, the aspect ratio of the facets on
>> different plots are different, something that works havoc on any
>> plot-
>> to-plot comparison.
>>
>> In standard R I would usually fix this by changing the device size,

>> Thanks

What is the proper method of flipping an Axis? The data I'm plotting is
right to left, not left to right, so I've been supplying a xlim with
flipped ranges:

qplot(data=pantilt3,x=pan,y=tilt,geom="path",colour=i,size=1,ylim=c(1600,2180),xlim=c(12500,4700))

as.numeric solution does not work because I do not want all points to
be connected by a line, but:

matrix to be one line (of length 50) in the plot which thus contains

x = matrix(rnorm(50*160),ncol=160)

Many thanks in advance,
Silke.

messages.subject_clean: A way to "lock down" the order of bars for ggplot "dodged" histogram
messages.body_plain:
It appears that ggplot reorder the data for a "dodged" histogram based on whether or not a specific variable has a value in the first bin.

I would like to be able to absolutely force the order of the variables in the bin.  For example, say I have three variables Me, You, and Them.

Me_df<-data.frame(Data = c(1:15), Person = "Me")
You_df<-data.frame(Data = c(10:20), Person = "You")
Them_df<-data.frame(Data = c(15:25), Person = "Them")
Group_df_tmp<-rbind(Me_df,You_df)
Group_df<-rbind(Group_df_tmp,Them_df)
counts <- ddply(Group_df, .(cut(Data, breaks=fullseq(range(Data), 5)), Person), nrow)
names(counts) <- c("Bin", "Person", "Frequency")
qplot(Person, Frequency, data = counts, fill = Person, geom="bar", stat="identity", width = 0.9, xlab="Person") +  facet_grid(. ~ Bin)

However, I absolutely must have the bar order be Them, You, Me.   Is there a to fix the order of the bars so that they are always in the Them, You, Me order?

Thank you again for any feedback you can provide.

messages.subject: datetime plot question
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm an occasional R user, trying to draw a simple time-series plot
with dates on the x-axis. Since I don't want to round everything to
the nearest day, I wanted to use the datetime scale instead of date.
But I'm getting an error I can't decipher -- "subscript out of
bounds". Below is an example of my problem. Can someone tell me the
right way to do this?

Thanks,

-Dan

> data <- data.frame(t = 1230797742 + runif(6, max = 100), v = runif(6))
> data
           t         v
1 1230797763 0.2538046
2 1230797823 0.6465227
3 1230797835 0.3853473
4 1230797804 0.5170273
5 1230797800 0.6793329
6 1230797829 0.2043300
> ISOdatetime(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, tz="") + t
[1] "2009-01-01 08:15:42 PST" "2009-01-01 08:20:47 PST" "2009-01-01
08:23:03 PST" "2009-01-01 08:23:13 PST"
[5] "2009-01-01 08:25:17 PST" "2009-01-01 08:28:39 PST"
> p <- ggplot(data, aes( x = ISOdatetime(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, tz="") + t, y = v))
> p + geom_point()
Error in labels[[i]] : subscript out of bounds
> qplot(ISOdatetime(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, tz="") + t, v, data=data)
Error in labels[[i]] : subscript out of bounds

messages.body_plain:
The suggestion below of using "opts" instead of "grid.gedit" seemed to fixed both problems.

I end up using the following to reduce the facet text size:
+ opts(strip.text.x = theme_text(size=7))

messages.subject: Re: datetime plot question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dang,

There's a bug in the current version of ggplot2 that crops up with
certain spans of time - the automatic break finding algorithm fails
with that strange error you see.  The solution is to manually specify
the major, minor and format arguments:

... + scale_x_datetime(major = "2 days", minor = "day", format = "%m/%d")

Regards,

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: opts(aspect.ratio) is incorrect
messages.body_plain:
That looks like a bug.  You can see it most simply with:

qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars)  + coord_equal()
qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars)  + coord_equal() + scale_x_reverse()

I'll it to my to do list.

Unfortunately there are non-trivial interactions between the scales
and the coordinate system that I don't have fully figured out yet.

You can work around the problem by plotting the negative of the value
and then using a custom breaks and labels.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: question on defaults for geom_smooth
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

There are two default methods for geom_smooth:

 * less than 1000 points, loess is used
 * more than 1000 points, mgcv::gam(y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")) is used

Yes, the confidence bands come from predict.loess or predict.gam, and
you'll probably need to read the cited papers to figure out exactly
how they are calculated.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: How often are ggplot versions released?
messages.subject_clean: How often are ggplot versions released?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,

There's not any particular release schedule - it all depends on how
much time I have to work on the code.  Lately, I've been trying to do
smaller, more frequent releases with some success, but it takes quite
a long time for me to run all the tests to make sure I haven't broken
anything from the previous version.  Unfortunately this currently
involves a significant manual component (inspecting many plots to make
sure they look ok) and is both slow and rather error prone.

The development version currently contains about 20 bug fixes and
other small changes.  I'll probably try to release this as soon as I
send the book off for copy editing (hopefully this weekend!)

Hadley

It's the commands that you're using.  With the qplot() command you're creating the plot with the dots, then you are adding a layer with the X's above it.  I think either of the following commands is what you want :

df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y), data = df) +
  geom_point(shape = I(4))

or

qplot(x, y, data = df, geom = 'point', shape = I(4))

messages.subject: Re: using stat_function() to produce simple plots
messages.subject_clean: using stat_function() to produce simple plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Russ,

I'd never really thought about using stat_function for that purpose -
it's basically designed to work with on top of an existing plot.
However, it's pretty easy to make a little function to do what you
want:

fplot <- function(f, .min, .max, ..., .n = 100) {
  x <- seq(.min, .max, length = .n)
  y <- f(x, ...)

  qplot(x, y, data = data.frame(x, y), geom = "line")
}

fplot(dnorm, -3, 3, mean = 0, sd = 1)

(I use . in front of min and max so that you don't inadvertently match
those arguments instead of the arguments of the function that your
plotting)

If you wanted to go even further and automatically come up with good
default limits for the plot, you could use the ideas in here:
http://www.cs.uic.edu/~wilkinson/Publications/plotfunc.pdf

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: jaggies
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

A related question has been itching me for a while, I'd be curious to hear opinions about this (copied from a post to R-help that received no answer).

My favorite output format is usually pdf. I can include the graphics in pdflatex documents and benefit from the scalable nature of vector graphic formats.
However, I recently had to generate high-res 2D levelplot graphics as in the example below,

N <- 100
# N <- 1000 # slow to render, made my MacBook Pro unusable for minutes
xy <- expand.grid(x=seq(0, 10, length=N), y=seq(0, 10, length=N))

xy <- within(xy, z <- x^2*cos(x*y))

library(ggplot2)

p <- qplot(x, y, data = xy, geom = "tile", fill = z)

pdf("plot.pdf")
print(p)
dev.off()

png("plot.png")
print(p)
dev.off()

With N=1000, this approach produces a hefty pdf file of ~39MB (similar lattice output was 29MB for some reason), while the png file with default resolution is only 164kB. It is clear that I don't want to include the pdf figure in a manuscript, as most pdf readers (let alone the printer) will painfully stall when scrolling down the document. The png file has a good enough resolution (this could be tuned anyway) as far as the levelplot is concerned, however the text and labels are evidently converted to bitmap. I would like to ask whether there are some alternative ways to combine the "best of both worlds" in ggplot or R in general, that is to create a pdf file with part of the output being an embedded bitmap (the levelplot in this case). Xfig, as I recall, has a way to produce two separate files for this kind of purpose: one containing the graphical information stripped of annotations, the other the labels and axes to be processed by TeX. Because of the layer and object approach in grid graphics, it seems that it ought to be possible to create two such temporary files with exactly the same dimensions and combine them into a light-weight, mixed type pdf. Such a feature, even experimental, would be very neat and useful.

On a side note, I noticed that Acrobat Professional can substantially reduce the file size, but it does not seem to help some pdf readers (Preview on Leopard, for one). I'm open to suggestions of auxiliary tools that might help.

Best regards,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Functions that create ggplot2 plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley,

I've only tried this once, mostly because I am uneasy about the scoping and parsing rules when passing arguments to a plot from within a function. On the plus side, ggplot is probably the best approach I know of to return a plot object that you can subsequently modify by adding layers, etc.

The following function (package constants on r-forge/photonics) takes a data.frame, does some trivial conversion, and outputs a list containing a ggplot. A few bottlenecks I've encountered:

- in an interactive session, calling the result of this function will print the plot whether I want it or not. I'm not sure how to make it more invisible.

- the variable names in the ggplot call are all hard-wired because I don't know how to pass them as arguments. A few tips on using substitute, quote, bquote, eval, deparse ... would be very useful I think.

- a slight issue with plotmath type labels not working in strips, but this is not relevant here

material2plot <- function(material, xaxis="wavelength"){
    mdf <- with(material, {data.frame(
        lambda=lambda, energy = L2eV(lambda),
        epsr=Re(epsilon),  epsi=Im(epsilon),
        n=Re(nk),  k=Im(nk))
        })

    meltdf <- melt(mdf, id.var=c("lambda", "energy"))

    levels(meltdf$variable) <- c(expression(epsilon[r]), expression(epsilon[i]), expression(n), expression(k))
    mqplot <- ggplot(data = meltdf, mapping = aes(x = lambda, y = value)) + facet_wrap(~variable, scale="free") +
    layer(data=meltdf, mapping=aes(colour=variable),  geom = c( "line"), stat = "identity" )  +
    scale_y_continuous("") +
    scale_colour_brewer(palette="Set1")
    if(xaxis == "wavelength"){
        mqplot <- mqplot +
        scale_x_continuous(expression("wavelength / "*mu*m))
    }else{
        mqplot <- mqplot +
            scale_x_continuous(expression("energy / eV"))
}
    invisible(list(mdf=mdf, meltdf=meltdf, qplot=mqplot))
}

# example
data(AuJChristy) # load some raw data
gold <- fit.material("AuJChristy", range=c(0.4, 1), draw=F) # create the data.frame used in material2plot (spline fit of the raw data)

material2plot(gold$fine)->testFine
material2plot(gold$raw)->testRaw

testFine # this prints the plot in an interactive session

testFine$qplot + # this possibility of adding layers is awesome!
layer(data=testRaw$meltdf, mapping=aes(colour=variable),  geom = c( "point"), stat = "identity" )

messages.body_plain:
> I've only tried this once, mostly because I am uneasy about the scoping and
> parsing rules when passing arguments to a plot from within a function. On
> the plus side, ggplot is probably the best approach I know of to return a
> plot object that you can subsequently modify by adding layers, etc.

You will always be ok provided all of the data you provide in a data
frame.  If you use ggplot you should almost always be ok, unless you
are using local variables in an aes call (which is theoretically not
allowed but I can't figure out how to detect it so I can issue an
error)

> The following function (package constants on r-forge/photonics) takes a
> data.frame, does some trivial conversion, and outputs a list containing a
> ggplot. A few bottlenecks I've encountered:
>
> - in an interactive session, calling the result of this function will print
> the plot whether I want it or not. I'm not sure how to make it more
> invisible.

What I would do here is split your function into two pieces - one that
creates the data frame and one that produces the plot.  This makes it
much easier for other people to build on top of your efforts if they
don't want to use any part of the plot you provide (at least they can
get the data separately from the plot in your function, which is
better than most of base R)

So I'd suggest material2plot just returns a list of the two data
frames with class = "material2plot".  You then write a
plot.material2plot that produces the plot.  Your example would then
become:

gold <- fit.material("AuJChristy", range=c(0.4, 1), draw=F)

material2plot(gold$fine)->testFine

plot(testFine)
plot(testFine) + geom_point(aes(colour = variable))

> - the variable names in the ggplot call are all hard-wired because I don't
> know how to pass them as arguments. A few tips on using substitute, quote,
> bquote, eval, deparse ... would be very useful I think.

Ok - aes_string is probably the way to go here.  aes_string("x",
"myvar") is equivalent to aes(x, myvar), with the obvious difference
that it's much much much easier to work with strings than expressions.

> is not relevant here

messages.subject: Plotting marginal and conditional distributions: layouts and viewports in grid
messages.subject_clean: Plotting marginal and conditional distributions: layouts and viewports in grid
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In an effort to learn Grid graphics (so as to be able to tweak
ggplot), I put together some code to plot marginal and conditional
distributions using viewports and layouts.
The resulting plot captures the intent, but a lot of it still does not
make sense. I am hoping someone could give me pointers to things that
I am missing.

Issues:

(a) grid.lines() instead of grid.points() blows the layout/viewports
entirely.
(b) I suppose I could add "viewports' for axis and labels of the
marginal distributions.
(c) Ideally, I would like to do this using ggplot. There was some
discussion in the list that aligning axes is problematic.
(d) The current approach is too low-level. While a function wouldl
make it more general, it seems that all of the pieces have a higher-
level description. From ggplot's perspective, the description should
be adequate to produce such plots.
(e) Any pointers regarding the aesthetic aspects of such plotting
would be appreciated.

Thanks.

~Russ

x <- seq(-3,3,length=100)
y <- seq(-3,3,length=100)
dx <- dnorm(x)
dy <- dnorm(y)
m  <- 1.5
sd <- .5
.min <- m - 2*sd
.max <- m + 2*sd
y2<-seq(.min,.max,length=100)
cd_y <-dnorm(y2,m=1.5,sd=.5)

xs <-extendrange(x)
ys <-extendrange(y)
dxs <-extendrange(dx)
dys <-extendrange(dy)
cdys <-extendrange(cd_y)

grid.newpage()
grid.rect()
mylayout <- grid.layout(2, 2,
  widths  = unit(c(0.5,1.0)*3, c("inches", "inches")),
  heights = unit(c(1.0,0.5)*3, c("inches", "inches")), respect=TRUE)

top.vp <- viewport(layout = mylayout,
            name = "top.vp",
            width=1,
            height=1)

marginal_y1 <- viewport(layout.pos.col = 1, layout.pos.row = 1,
                name = "marginal_y1")
marginal_y2 <- viewport(width = 2, height = .5, angle=90,
                name = "marginal_y2",
                xscale = ys, yscale = dys)

marginal_x1 <- viewport(layout.pos.col = 2, layout.pos.row = 2,
                name = "marginal_x1")
marginal_x2 <- viewport(name = "marginal_x2",
                xscale = xs, yscale = dxs,
                angle=180)

line_xy <- viewport(layout.pos.col = 2, layout.pos.row = 1,
            name = "line_xy",
            xscale = xs, yscale = ys,
            clip="on")

cond_y1 <- viewport(x=unit(1.5,"native"),y=unit(1.5,"native"),
            height = unit(1,"native"),width=unit(2,"native"),
            name = "cond_y1",
            just=c("center","bottom"),
            angle=-90)

cond_y2 <- viewport(name = "cond_y2",
            xscale = extendrange(y2), yscale = cdys)

splot <- vpTree(top.vp,
                    vpList(
                        vpStack(marginal_y1,marginal_y2),
                        vpStack(marginal_x1,marginal_x2),
                        vpStack(line_xy,
                            vpStack(cond_y1,cond_y2))))

pushViewport(splot)
grid.rect()

seekViewport("line_xy")
grid.lines(x, y)
 grid.xaxis()
 grid.yaxis()
 grid.rect()

seekViewport("marginal_y2")
grid.points(y, dy)
 grid.xaxis()
 grid.rect()

seekViewport("marginal_x2")
grid.points(x, dx)
 grid.xaxis()
 grid.rect()

seekViewport("cond_y2")
grid.points(y2, cd_y)
 grid.xaxis()

messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley,

Thanks for the useful advice on this. I'm afraid this wasn't much of an example on how to use ggplot2 in a function though! I agree on the good practice that is separating the data manipulation and the plotting, but it probably means that creating a ggplot in a function is not very common. In fact, ggplot2 is so high-level that it's hard to see how it could be abstracted much further in a wrap-up function. Rggobi is probably a good example of generating ggplot code automatically but you don't need input for this!

Two related problems that require more low-level user adaptations come to mind, but it's not directly answering your query,

1) create a custom layout using grid, and place several ggplots in it. That's an area where many tricky questions can arise (how to align two plots with respect to their x-axis, how to put a legend in another viewport, generalize the facet_wrap layout, how to add an inset inside a ggplot? ...)

2) create a new object that you haven't implemented yet and use it in a plot. I'm thinking of a new grob such as a secondary x-axis for instance, or a new geom, ...

I'm a novice re both R and ggplot2, so apologies if this is a naive

Here's a few lines from the kind of data set that causes me the
problem:

   gender   dosage perf
1    male     zero   10
2    male     zero   10
3    male     zero    8
...

where gender and dosage are factors.

Then I try  this to get something like a simple interaction plot:

> p <- ggplot(data=testdataset)
> p + stat_summary(fun=mean, mapping=aes(x=dosage, y=perf, colour=gender, group=gender), geom="line")

which gives me this error:

Error in as.data.frame.default(x[[i]], optional = TRUE) :
  cannot coerce class "labelled" into a data.frame

One odd thing is that in an earlier R session exactly the same
commands did produce a plot without error, on exactly the same data
set (though I didn't keep my R history, so perhaps there's a subtle
difference I'm missing).

Any idea what I might be doing wrong?

Cheers,

CB.

messages.body_plain:
Good morning Hadley,

Perhaps it might help you if you were to release the test plots side
by side with plots from a previous release into a betatest page (or
release candidate) and then send an email to this list (or a special
ggplot2 beta-testing list) asking for help in regression testing the
plots?  If the plots are clearly numbered to ease bug reports, and if
there is a bug fix in the new version that this is labeled as such to
avoid any unnecessary bug reports.  Should beta-testing bug-reports go
to this list or a separate bug-reporting list?

For those of us with less experience in the technical side of
plotting, this visual comparison testing could be a useful way of
contributing?  I'd guess that you could release much more often in a
more "agile" way.  If a beta-release lasts say 24hrs without any
significant issues then it could be auto-released?  Thoughts?  I'd
imagine a folder for each release and the betatest page could show
comparisons between folders?

Since disk space and bandwidth have reduced significantly in price,
I'd now err on the side of over-production of tests, though I
appreciate that some people are still on slower connections.

Could be a first live outing for your Sweave-lilke project? :-)

Kind Regards,
Sean O'Riordain

Hi all,

I'm currently producing lots of graphs and when I finally submit my thesis i'm planning to put together a webpage with all the figures and the code to produce them (a bit iffy to give away my work until it's submitted/published). Here's a link to the format I have in mind,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean,

> Perhaps it might help you if you were to release the test plots side
> by side with plots from a previous release into a betatest page (or
> release candidate) and then send an email to this list (or a special
> ggplot2 beta-testing list) asking for help in regression testing the
> plots?  If the plots are clearly numbered to ease bug reports, and if
> there is a bug fix in the new version that this is labeled as such to

That is a great idea and I have tried to do so.  However, there is one
huge problem which I have not been able to resolve - how do you label
or number the plots so that the labels are consistent across versions,
even when their position in the example changes.  In the current code
there is a digest.ggplot method which attempts to calculate a hash
code for each plot, based on all the plot components.  This is ok in
principle, but in practice I always end up making some change to the
plot structure so that every plot gets a new hash code and I can't
match the plots from one version to another.

> avoid any unnecessary bug reports.  Should beta-testing bug-reports go
> to this list or a separate bug-reporting list?

Either to this list or to me.  I don't want to swamp people with bug
reports for bugs they encounter, but on the other hand it's amazing
the number of duplicate bug reports I receive.

> For those of us with less experience in the technical side of
> plotting, this visual comparison testing could be a useful way of
> contributing?  I'd guess that you could release much more often in a
> more "agile" way.  If a beta-release lasts say 24hrs without any
> significant issues then it could be auto-released?  Thoughts?  I'd
> imagine a folder for each release and the betatest page could show
> comparisons between folders?

Yes, I think that's a really good idea, and you can speed things up
even further by not showing any plots that are identical between
versions - it's then up to a human to decide whether or not the
differences are significant.  That would go a long way to ensuring
that I don't introduce new bugs in a new version, but I'm not sure if
it would speed up the release process much - after all the changes are
completed you still have to rerun all the plots to make sure you
haven't introduced any new bugs when fixing the old bugs.

As I get closer to version 1.0, I hope I'll be able to spend some time
optimising the code.  I'm confident I should be able to get at least
2-3x fold speed up, which will make producing all the sample graphics
that much faster.

Hadley

as well as in the layout.

I don't use this style of grid, so I can't give you much help.
Instead of manually moving around the viewport stack, I use the vp
parameter to supply the name of the viewport to each grob.

Yes, and it's tricky.  I draw a lot of diagrams and spending a lot of
time working out the details.

> discussion in the list that aligning axes is problematic.

supply those plots as arguments to your function as well as parameters

It's hard to do it nicely!

I actually wanted to do a function using ggplot2 because I was doing
about 10 plots that were all variations on the same theme and each had
similar text annotations. Mostly what stopped me was that I didn't
understand how to deal with formulas in functions. (And "formula"
turns out to be an unhelpful search term because it covers so much.) I
needed to create a formula both for cast() and for qplot() such as
"year + group + class ~ amt".  I am new enough to R that I don't
understand whether formula is a general class or whether a formula
like this is specific to ggplot2.  What I wanted to do was pass some
of this to the function and then have the function built the formula.
Your comment to baptiste's message about using aes_string rather than
aes() is what I needed to know, I think. I'd have an analogous issue
with cast(), and it looks like I could try cast_parse_formula for
that.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was looking at writing a convenience function for creating
histograms of integer elements (and also provide an example in
response to Hadley's request), but my function seems to lock up R.
Here's the function:

library(ggplot2)
intHist <- function(x, xlab=xlab, main=main) {
  d <- data.frame(x=x)
  r <- range(x)
  print(qplot(x, data=d, breaks=seq(r[1] - 0.5, r[2] + 0.5, by=1),
xlab=xlab, main=main, geom="histogram"))
}

After defining this, in R 2.8.1 with ggplot2 0.8.1 on a MacBook Pro,
executing the following causes R to freeze:

intHist(c(1,1,2,2,2))

Any ideas? Thanks.

David

One problem which was killing it was how you defaulted xlab - it needs to be xlab = 'xlab'  in quotes (the axis label's a character string, see below).  Otherwise, when it tries to evoke it, it will start looking for the variable xlab, and it won't find it.  It was making it hang on my computer; probably the same on yours.

>  promise already under evaluation: recursive default argument
> reference or earlier problems?

One fix to do what you want is to change the integers to factors.  I've tried this and it seems to do just what you want on my computer.  Let me know if it's what you're looking for.

x <- sample(10,100, replace = T)

intHist <- function(x, xlab = 'x', main = '') {
  d <- data.frame(x=factor(x))
  ggplot(aes(x=x), data = d) +
    stat_bin(breaks = seq(min(x), max(x), 1), width = .5) +
    scale_x_discrete(xlab) +
    opts(title = main)
}
intHist(x)
intHist(x, xlab = 'text x', main = 'test main')

Cheers

messages.subject: question facet_wrap versus coord_cartesian
messages.body_plain:
Dear all !

My question can most easily be understood by the following example:

DM<-diamonds
p<-ggplot(mapping=aes(x = carat, y = price))
p<- p + coord_cartesian(xlim=NULL, ylim=c(0,5000))
p<-p+geom_point(data=DM )
p<-p+facet_wrap(~ cut,ncol=2)
p

In other words: I want to zoom on (but not filter) a part of the given
data (ylim=c(0,5000)) and afterwards use this zoom for the facet_wrap
which however produces the above result.
Since with facet_grid instead of facet_wrap it works perfectly my
question is if this is a bug or what can be done to make the
coordinate-settings also work in the facet_grid.

Thanks in advance and best regards

Wolfgang

j <- as.POSIXct(j)
p <- qplot(j,k)
print(p)

> I think that an automatic test name is not a good idea, instead each
> test should be numbered and name by hand by *intent* with the
> possibility of retiring tests that are no longer relevant.  So if you
> have new code that doesn't yet have an ancestor, then there is a blank
> space to the "left" where the ancestor would normally be.

Perhaps that would have been a good idea in the beginning (although it
would clutter up the examples a lot), but I have absolutely no desire
to go through and label all >300 existing examples :(

> I've been using R for auto-testing large numbers of account statements
> for a variety of things (don't ask!) and I've come to the conclusion
> that they must be numbered and named by hand.  So I say things like...
>
> testname <- "Test 1.35 (Critical) Names must match"
> # or...
> testname <- "Test 7.22 (Minor) trailing spaces on lines"
> etc...
>
> Where I try to group the tests by major and minor groups (left /
> right) of decimal point...
>
> <snip/>

>
>>> For those of us with less experience in the technical side of
>>> plotting, this visual comparison testing could be a useful way of
>>> contributing?  I'd guess that you could release much more often in a
>>> more "agile" way.  If a beta-release lasts say 24hrs without any
>>> significant issues then it could be auto-released?  Thoughts?  I'd
>>> imagine a folder for each release and the betatest page could show
>>> comparisons between folders?
>>
>> Yes, I think that's a really good idea, and you can speed things up
>> even further by not showing any plots that are identical between
>> versions - it's then up to a human to decide whether or not the
>> differences are significant.  That would go a long way to ensuring
>> that I don't introduce new bugs in a new version, but I'm not sure if
>> it would speed up the release process much - after all the changes are
>> completed you still have to rerun all the plots to make sure you
>> haven't introduced any new bugs when fixing the old bugs.
>

> Well if you can create a "batch" program to create all the test images
> (possibly more than one format)... each named in the same way each
> time... however you chose to do so...
>
> Then you run the batch and scan through it quickly yourself for
> glaring errors, then hit the upload.my.batch.of.test.images() function
> or is it a method? :-)... and auto.send.email.to.group()... and go to
> sleep for two hours... :-)  put it this way... lots of people can do
> testing simultaneously... on a "small" tight project like this only a
> small number of people can code.  So let the group help you with
> regression testing...

I have code to do this, it's the naming/numbering problem that's
holding me back - and I just don't see any solution that doesn't
require me to spend hours of effort manually labelling the plots.

Hadley

x <- sort(rnorm(47))
df1<-data.frame(y=x,x=seq_along(x),z='A')
x <- sort(rnorm(47))
df2<-data.frame(y=x,x=seq_along(x),z='B')
df <-rbind(df1,df2)
qplot(data=df,x=x,y=y,colour=z)+geom_step() #lines get scrambled
qplot(data=df,x=x,y=y,colour=z)+geom_line() #lines from different
groups are separated

Thanks a lot!

messages.subject: Re: suggestions for plotting this data
messages.body_plain:
I wouldn't use lines, since both your variables are categorical. I
also wouldn't recommend bars, as I've come across arguments that they
are less visually succinct (and possibly misleading) than points. With
a 2x2 design, just plot one IV on the x axis and vary the color &
shape of the points by the other IV.

With respect to error bars, humans (even knowledgeable researchers)
aren't very good at interpreting error bars that represent confidence
intervals. I prefer to use Fisher's Least Significant Difference as
the error bar, that way any points whose bars fail to overlap are
significantly different (but only if the plotted effect is significant
in the omnibus anova). The code below calculates the LSD bar of the
highest order interaction in a given aov object. To use it as a bar,
plot half the LSD on each side of each data point (ex.
p+error_bar(aes(ymin=y+this_lsd/2,ymax=y-this_lsd/2))  ).

CI <- function(N, MSE, MSEdf) {Tcrit<-qt(0.975,MSEdf); Tcrit * sqrt(MSE/N)}
LSD <- function(from.aov) {
	MSEdf=from.aov[length(from.aov)][[1]]$df.residual
	MSE=sum(from.aov[length(from.aov)][[1]]$residuals^2)/MSEdf
	N=summary(from.aov[[2]])[[1]]$Df+1
	sqrt(2) * CI(N,MSE,MSEdf)

}

messages.subject: Re: circular plots again
messages.body_plain:
Bruce,

Still not totally clear on what you're asking. Is the following example something like what you mean?

y <- runif (100, 0, 50)
x <- runif (100, 0, 359)
datapoints <- data.frame (x=x, y=y)

night <- data.frame (x=c(90, 90, 180, 180), y=c(0, 50, 50, 0))

qplot (x, y, data=datapoints) + geom_line (data=night)

Now, make it polar:

qplot (x, y, data=datapoints) + geom_line (data=night) + coord_polar ()

It's not a truly "circular" answer in that R and ggplot know nothing about your data actually wrapping around. Which means two things:

1. If you wanted, say, to plot a smoothed curve for your data, you'd have to either use a circular package that supports such things, or you'd want to append your data three times, offseting the time so that it repeats, then do your smooth, then have ggplot truncate down to only the proper range of data -- not showing the other two copies of the data off of the two ends that were only there to make the smoothed curve meet at the seam.

2. If you want to plot lines that wrap around through the seam... For example, if my "night" variable went from 300 to 30 (i.e. "390"), I'd have to manually break it into two lines at the seam, 300-359 and 0-30.

It's definitely doable, and once you figure it out, R lets you easily write functions that automate the work.

P.S. Hadley: ggplot2 makes this exercise MUCH easier than any other package! Basically, you get it to work in a standard Cartesian coordinate system, then throw on the coord_polar, and VOILA. (Actually, for the sake of complete disclosure, I have had a graph that works in Cartesian coords refuse to plot, with an error, when I threw it into Polar coordinates. I assume that was a bug at that particular time in ggplot history and it should always work...)

   Wayne

messages.body_plain:
Below I've included some handy date functions that I use.  With them
you can remove the date component of a date time as follows:

year(mydate) <- 2000
yday(mydate) <- 1

then when you plot mydate, you'll only see a days worth of data
(getting the day to start at 6am would be a little trickier, however)

second <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$sec
minute <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$min
hour <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$hour
yday <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$yday + 1
wday <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$wday + 1
mday <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$mday
week <- function(x) yday(x) %/% 7 + 1
month <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$mon + 1
year <- function(x) as.POSIXlt(x)$year + 1900
tz <- function(x) {
	tzs <- attr(as.POSIXlt(x),"tzone")
	tzs[length(tzs)]
}

"second<-" <- function(x, value) as.POSIXlt(x) - (second(x) - value)
"minute<-" <- function(x, value) as.POSIXlt(x) - (minute(x) - value) * 60
"hour<-" <- function(x, value) as.POSIXlt(x) - (hour(x) - value) * 3600
"yday<-" <- function(x, value) as.POSIXlt(x) - (yday(x) - value) * 3600 * 24
"wday<-" <- function(x, value) as.POSIXlt(x) - (wday(x) - value) * 3600 * 24
"mday<-" <- function(x, value) as.POSIXlt(x) - (mday(x) - value) * 3600 * 24
"week<-" <- function(x, value) as.POSIXlt(x) - (week(x) - value) * 3600 * 24 * 7
"month<-" <- function(x, value) {
	ISOdatetime(year(x) + (value - 1) %/% 12,  (value - 1) %% 12 + 1 ,
mday(x), hour(x), minute(x), second(x), tz(x))
}
"year<-" <- function(x, value) {
	ISOdatetime(value,  month(x), mday(x), hour(x), minute(x), second(x), tz(x))
}
"tz<-" <- function(x, value) {
	ISOdatetime(year(x),  month(x), mday(x), hour(x), minute(x), second(x), value)
}

Hadley

To be specific with my data:

> thresholds$category[1:5]
[1] Jython modules   Java             Jython compiler  Python
library   Python benchmark
Levels: Java Jython compiler Jython core Jython modules Python
benchmark Python library

The stacking order is that of the data (first to last, bottom to top);
the legend is sorted as with the levels. If I use:

thresholds$category = factor(thresholds$category, levels=rev(unique
(thresholds$category)))

as you suggest, I get the same ordering, though with different colors,
as the code I posted.

I realized in retrospect it was trivial to change the stacking order
by sorting the data, in this case to match the default levels:

thresholds = thresholds[order(thresholds$category, decreasing=TRUE),]

Hopefully my original question is now clearer. Is there a way to keep
the stacking order and legend order the same, or should I continue to
use sorting and reversing as above to match the observed behavior?

Thanks, and sorry for any confusion.

later)

library(Hmisc)
## barplot with error bars computed on the fly

(bpe)

I get the error:

> Error in x - from[1] : non-numeric argument to binary operator
In addition: Warning messages:

width=0.2)

Am I crazy?

messages.subject: ggplot2 0.8.2
messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 ------------------------------------------------------------

ggplot2 is a plotting system for R, based on the grammar of graphics,
which tries to take the good parts of base and lattice graphics and
avoid bad parts. It takes care of many of the fiddly details
that make plotting a hassle (like drawing legends) as well as
providing a powerful model of graphics that makes it easy to produce
complex multi-layered graphics.

Find out more at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2, and check out the nearly 500
examples of ggplot in use.  If you're interested, you can also sign up to
the ggplot2 mailing list at http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2, or track
development at http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2

ggplot2 0.8.2  (2008-02-23)
----------------------------------------

New features

* borders, fortify.map and map_data to make it easier to draw map
borders and choropleth maps

* cut_interval and cut_number utility functions to discretise
continuous variables

* stat_summary has reparameterised to make it easier to specify
different summary functions.  It now has four parameters: fun.y,
fun.ymin and fun.ymax; and fun.data.  See the documentation for
stat_summary for more details

Minor improvements

* ggfluctuation: default to aspect ratio that produces squares
* ggsave: filename now first parameter, not second
* qplot: if sample aesthetic is used, stat automatically set to qq
* scale_datetime: improved breaks calculation
* scale_gradient: better default colour scheme from red to blue
(thanks to Charlotte Wickham for providing the Munsell colours)
* scale_size and scale_area: increased default size range
* stats: all give useful error message if missing a required aesthetic
* theme_set warns if missing needed theme elements
* theme_text: now possible to right and left align text with hjust=0
and hjust=1 respectively

Bug fixes

* be explicit about plyr::is.discrete to avoid clash with Hmisc
* facet_wrap: work around R bug so no longer crashers when ncol = 1
* geom_errorbar now works correctly with dashed lines
* geom_path will now silently ignore lines with less than 2 points
(instead of throwing a mysterious error as before)
* geom_path now responds to the size aesthetic once more
* geom_polygon etc now correctly displays linetype on legends
* geom_step now works with multiple groups
* geom_vline and geom_hline: fix bug when mapping intercept to
variable in data frame
* ggsave: path parameter correctly sets path
* guides: fix broken legend from default stat aesthetics (e.g. for stat_sum)
* scale_manual now works better with missing values
* scale_manual: labels now correctly sets legend labels.
* stat_density_2d: no longer passes unnecessary parameters to kde2d
causing an error message (seen when setting aesthetics with qplot)
* stat_pointrange: better relationship between point and line widths
* stat_sum now correctly preserves other aesthetic columns (should be
a bit faster too)

Regards,

Hadley

--

messages.subject: unexpected ordering behaviour from facet_grid
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Apologies if this is simply something I'm doing wrong or is a known
issue but I am encountering unexpected ordering behaviour from
facet_grid when faceting a histogram where the first facet is empty,
i.e. no members. To illustrate I've uploaded an extract of my data
file and three jpegs to the "files" section of the group (hope that
works, not something I've done before).

The data file records the ages of patients seen in a clinic over a two
year period (2007 & 2008), with age ready-binned into 4 groups (<40,
40-64, 65-79, & 80+). I just want to facet the data by year to show
the histograms for each year side by side, but qplot puts the age bins
in the wrong order:

library(ggplot2)
qplot(AgeCut4, data = facet_problem_data, geom="histogram") +
facet_grid(. ~ Year) #puts the age bins in the wrong order: see jpeg
#1

Yet lattice has no such trouble

library(lattice)
histogram(~AgeCut4|Year, data=facet_problem_data, type="count") #no
bin labels: but at least has the bins in the right order: see jpeg #2

The problem seems to be that there were were no patients aged <40 in
2007 and thus the first facet (2007: <40) is empty. Adding a dummy
patient aged <40 in 2007 switches the order of the age bins the right
way round again: see jpeg #3

facet_problem_data$AgeCut4=ordered(facet_problem_data$AgeCut4, c
("<40", "40-64", "65-79", "80+")) #Ordering the variable does not help

qplot(AgeCut4, data = facet_problem_data, geom="histogram") +
facet_grid(Year ~ .) #Faceting by row not column does not help

?

Best

Andrew Graham

messages.subject: Re: About Bar chart
messages.body_plain:
On 25 Feb 2009, at 7:53 PM, teragene wrote:

> I am just a beginner of ggplot2.
> I want fill color to specific bar (different color for only some
> groups).
> I mean I have 9 bar on the graph. I want fill blue to 3 bars and fill
> red to 1 bar, rest of bars grey.
> Would you advise me what option I can apply?

I almost got this working (thought it was going to be easy), see
question on scale_fill_manual below.

Given this data in a file:

name, grade, section
student1, 56, A
student2, 68, A
student3, 58, A
student4, 99, B
student5, 46, C
student6, 44, C
student7, 34, C
student8, 56, C
student9, 76, C

Where 'section' is the categorical variable which is going to control
the color of the bars, this code is a start for you:

testdata <- read.csv("test-data.csv")
p <- ggplot(data=testdata,aes(x=name, y=grade,fill=section))
p + geom_bar()

So far so good.

Now the question is, how do I specifically control the colors used for
the bars?  You want to map A to blue, B to read and C to grey.

I tried this, based on the documentation of scale_manual, but
disappointingly it didn't work (got a nice legend, but no bars!)

p + geom_bar() + scale_fill_manual(values = c("A" = "blue","B" =
"red","C" = "grey"))

perhaps this has something to do with the section values being factors
whereas in the example the values are continuous? Anyone finish this
off?

Now it may be that you have to add a column to your data, or reshape
it (see ?melt) so that it matches this type of data table, so that you
have a variable to control the color of your bars.

If you need to manually control the order of your bars then you need
to treat testdata$name as an ordered factor, eg moving student7 to the
left:

testdata$name <- factor(testdata$name,
levels
=
c
("student7
","student1","student2","student3","student4","student5","student6",
"student8","student9",ordered=T))

hth,
James

ps. To get better answers try to provide some sample data and the code
that you've already tried, plus the documentation you read and why it
didn't help; that way everyone can learn something from your issues,
even if it's just how to explain things better :)

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a two questions.

1.  I have data for each day of weather for a complete calendar year.
Below is the code that I used to create a graph of weather. I don't
know what code to use to distance between the max and and the min to
be shaded, while the mean still stands out as a sort of trend line.
To this end, do you have any suggestions that might be 'better than'
the mean to show trend? I'm brand new to ggplot 2, so please be
gentle!
x<-read.csv("weather.csv")
plot(x$Day,x$Meantmp,type='l',main="Mean temperature for
2007",xlab="Day",ylab="",ylim=c(20,120),xlim=c(1,365))
lines(x$Day,x$Mntemp,col=”blue”)
lines(x$Day,x$Mxtmp,col=”red”)
color<-c(“blue”,”black”,”red”)
legend(2,120,c("---INDICATES LOW”, "---INDICATES MEAN TEMP”,"---
INDICATES HIGH”), col=color,text.col=color)

2.  Given that I have data for each day and I can use the attach(x)
feature to assign a the column title the numerical values in that
column; however, what I want to do is create a monthly histogram with
the actual precipitation (in.) for that month in one bar collected a
column in my csv file and in the other bar I want to manually insert
the average precipitation (in.) for each respective month.  In
addition, I would like each histogram to be labeled for each
respective month (i.e. January, February, etc.).

I really appreciate your help and feedback.

Thank you!

messages.subject: geom_vline and log y axis
messages.body_plain:

I'm trying to draw vertical lines in a CFD plot which uses log y
axis.  The line works no problems with a linear axis but doesn't like
the log transformation. I'm guessing there is an undefined problem for
y=0 and I have tried to limit y >= 1 but it does not seem to produce
the results I had intended.

pm10 <- read.csv("data.csv")
 h <- hist(pm10$x, breaks=100, plot=FALSE)

m <- qplot( h.mids,h.counts, data = yframe, geom="line",
xlab="Concentration",
            ylab = "Number of Periods where Concentration is > C",
            main = "Cumulative Frequency Distribution")
m <- m + geom_vline(xintercept=c(50,70))
m <- m + geom_hline(colour="darkblue", yintercept=c(5,10))
m <- m + ylim(2,365)
m <- m + coord_trans(y ="log10")
m

Is there a better way to draw in the vertical lines?

Cheers

Adrian

library (maptools)

maskpoly <- readShapeSpatial ('maskpoly08_general')

# extract data of interest
plotvar <- who3@data$inc_all

# prepare breaks and colours
nclr <- 6
plotclr <- brewer.pal (nclr, 'BuPu')
class <- classIntervals(plotvar, nclr, style="fixed",
            fixedBreaks=c(0,20,50,100,200,500,1200))
colcode <- findColours (class, plotclr)

# plot map and legend
plot (who3, col=colcode)
legend(-170, -25, legend=names(attr(colcode, "table")),
    fill=attr(colcode, "palette"), cex=0.6, bty="n")

# add disputed borders to the plot
plot (maskline, add=T)
plot (maskpoly, add=T)

messages.subject: Re: map_data ()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phillippe,

Below, I've included some code I've used previously for turning shape
files into data frames.  It doesn't work with the lines, but does with
your other two shapefiles. (It should also work for cases where each
main region is composed of multiple polygons, if you adapt the line
beginning with polys <-). The main problem is for such large datasets
you really need to be able thin (aka generalise) the map boundaries
and there isn't any code in R to do so, and so far my attempts to
write a topologically consistent polyline simplification algorithm
have not been successful.

Hadley

library(plyr)
library(gpclib)

invert <- function (L) {
  t1 <- unlist(L)
  names(t1) <- rep(names(L), lapply(L, length))
  tapply(names(t1), t1, c)
}

get_attributes <- function(shape) {
  attr <- as.data.frame(shape)
  names(attr) <- tolower(names(attr))

  attr
}

get_borders <- function(shape) {
  attr <- get_attributes(shape)
  cp <- polygons(shape)

  # Figure out how polygons should be split up into the region of interest
  # Currently just assume that this given by the first variable in the
  # attributes
  polys <- split(as.numeric(row.names(attr)), list(attr[, 1]))

  # Union together all polygons that make up a region
  unioned <- unionSpatialPolygons(cp, invert(polys))

  # Extract coordinates of regions
  get_coords <- function(x) {
    df <- as.data.frame(x@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[1]]@coords)
    names(df) <- c("long", "lat")
    df
  }
  coords <- llply(seq_along(polys), function(i) get_coords(unioned[i]))

  thinned <- coords

  # Add column to identify region
  named <- mlply(cbind(df = thinned, id = names(polys)),
    function(df, id) transform(df, id = id))

  do.call("rbind", named)
}

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
> Working through the book, and the diamond data is there but where do
> I find the sample mtcars data.

It's included with the package, as are the other sample datasets. Just
typing

 > mtcars

at the prompt should show you the data itself.

> Also I am getting errors when I try the commands from the PDF book.
>
> > p <- p + layer(geom = "point")
> > layer(geom, geom params, stat, stat params, data, mapping, position)
> Error: unexpected symbol in "layer(geom, geom params"
> >

If you copy and paste directly from the PDF you will likely leave the
underscores behind. So in this case you probably need,

 > layer(geom, geom_params, stat, stat_params, data, mapping, position)

Note the underscores.

Kieran
